claims.awareness_evidence: Experiment 4 tested contracting-motion presence after the RSVP task: participants reported whether the display included contracting dots. The supplement identifies 5% as below the mean chance-level threshold. Experiment 5 adds explicitly perception-linked instructions: report whether any coherent motion was perceived; detection performance increased with coherence. These reports address the proposed X, unlike direction discrimination. However, numerical detection results and uncertainty bounds are not supplied. Chance-level performance does not establish unawareness, and increasing objective accuracy alone does not establish consciousness. Jointly, these observations support a plausible lower-/higher-access comparison, not a demonstrated unconscious/conscious division. Transfer from Experiment 5 is limited by its six-person sample, separate task days, and removal of central RSVP demands; sample overlap is unspecified.
claims.comparison: In Experiment 4, 15 participants identified central digits while irrelevant contracting-motion coherence varied. RSVP d′ at 5% was lower than at 0%, 10%, and 20%. The awareness test used motion-presence judgments rather than digit identification. Shared methods place that test after the main task, with a fixation point replacing the RSVP sequence.
claims.contribution_reasoning: The useful observation is poorer digit identification with weak, reportedly below-threshold contraction than with stronger contraction. This reverses the straightforward prediction that stronger physical distractor signals simply produce greater interference. Contracting motion also reduces the translating-eye-movement explanation. The contribution is a bounded relationship between perceptual accessibility of irrelevant motion and interference with another task, not evidence that awareness independently causes suppression. The aligned presence judgment makes this narrower comparison worth retaining despite uncertain awareness classification.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Experiment 4 threshold instructions and Fig. S2 caption
decisive_evidence.observation: Presence judgments contrasted random dots with contracting-motion displays. At 5%, RSVP d′ was lower than at 0% (p < 0.01), 10% (p < 0.05), and 20% (p < 0.001); the caption places 5% below the mean chance-level threshold.

Experiment 4 used 15 participants. In Experiment 5, six participants showed maximal task-irrelevant MT+ activity at 5%, whereas task-relevant MT+ activity and detection performance increased with coherence.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Shared threshold procedure and Experiment 5 main-task instructions
decisive_evidence.observation: The shared post-task threshold procedure used 915-ms displays without RSVP. Experiment 5 requested reports of perceived coherent-motion presence, with relevant and irrelevant tasks on separate, counterbalanced days.

claims.downstream_use: Y is interference with central digit identification, measured by RSVP d′. It is not direct discrimination of the distractor. No direction-specific or symbolic use of motion is established.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Retain as a limited prospect. Human vetting should judge whether the content-aligned presence reports and threshold description sufficiently support a provisional accessibility comparison, without treating threshold labels as proof of subjective invisibility.
claims.remaining_alternative: Coherence changes the focal input; internal evidence is not matched. Nonlinear motion processing, ambiguity-dependent competition, or detection attempts could produce the interference peak without awareness-dependent inhibitory control. MT+ and LPFC observations are compatible with inhibition but do not establish it causally.
claims.supported_claim: Weak contracting-motion distractors impaired digit identification more than stronger contracting distractors, with a plausibly aligned but incompletely characterized awareness comparison.
claims.x_and_existence: X is the presence of coherent contracting motion. Controlled signal-dot generation establishes its physical presence; the behavioral interference and motion-sensitive activity support processing. Its exact neural representation is not established.

claims.awareness_evidence: Experiments 1–3 measured perceived translating-motion direction after RSVP. The actual threshold test used different directions and coherence levels from the main task. The article calls 5% chance-level, but that finding neither proves unconsciousness nor measures awareness of coherent-motion presence.
claims.comparison: Experiment 1, n = 15, compared translating distractors across coherence levels. Experiment 2, n = 10, lowered dot luminance and shifted both the reported threshold and interference dip toward higher coherence.
claims.contribution_reasoning: These experiments establish interpretable nonmonotonic interference and sensitivity to stimulus strength. They do not establish the required awareness comparison for the conservative presence-to-interference mapping. Keeping X as direction instead does not help: RSVP impairment does not demonstrate use of which direction was presented.

decisive_evidence.observation: RSVP d′ at 5% was lower than at 0% and 20% (both p < 0.001). Lower luminance shifted the dip to 30%, below performance at 20% and 40% (both p < 0.01).
Participants selected the arrow representing perceived direction; testing sampled 4%, 11%, 18%, 25%, 32%, 39%, and 46%, rather than directly sampling 5%.

claims.downstream_use: Digit-identification interference demonstrates distraction by the motion display, not use of its particular direction.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Context because the demonstrated downstream function and measured awareness content do not align. Vetting should not reinterpret failed direction discrimination as invisibility of motion presence.
claims.remaining_alternative: Participants could perceive motion presence without identifying direction. Threshold tracking can reflect sensory sensitivity rather than awareness-dependent control.
claims.supported_claim: Translating-motion interference peaks at intermediate signal strength, but its supplied awareness test concerns a different property from the demonstrated use.
claims.x_and_existence: Coherent translating motion is physically present. Its direction is experimentally specified, but direction-specific downstream use is not demonstrated.

Nonsignificant stronger-motion versus baseline differences do not demonstrate complete filtering or equivalence.

claims.awareness_evidence: After discrimination, Guess/Seen asked whether the Up/Down decision was a mere guess or based on some awareness: 43% Seen in the normal field versus 3% in the blind field. This is content-linked access reporting, not awareness of correctness. Reports and wagers occurred in separate, interleaved same-day blocks using the same stimuli and contrasts, making condition-level transfer reasonable but not trial-specific. Historical descriptions support absent blind-field visual qualia, while described Schurger studies report awareness that something was presented. These unavailable originals and the broad prompt caution against treating the blind regime as wholly unconscious.
claims.comparison: Independent contrast staircases targeted approximately 75% discrimination accuracy; achieved overall accuracy was 76% normal versus 79% blind. This is positive bounded performance control, not equivalence inferred from p=0.34. Normal-field contrast was much lower. Similar wager frequencies, 66% versus 69% (p=0.32), do not establish equal metacognitive capacity. The extreme-contrast comparison challenges a simple stronger-input/better-monitoring explanation for this same Y.
claims.contribution_reasoning: The directly tested difference in accuracy-sensitive wagering supplies a downstream behavioral contribution beyond stimulus discrimination or neural activation. Active titration and the extreme-contrast result constrain explanations based solely on physical strength or average discrimination success. The defensible contribution is an association between greater reported visual access and better metacognitive use, not independent causation by awareness, necessity, or equality of unconscious and conscious capacities.

decisive_evidence.observation: Gratings appeared for 500 ms, followed by Up/Down discrimination and then either wagering or Guess/Seen. Independently titrated contrasts produced 76% versus 79% overall accuracy; blind-field Guess trials were 74% correct.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Differences between hemifields in the capacity for metacognition
decisive_evidence.observation: Wager–accuracy correlations were 0.52 normal versus 0.30 blind, with a direct Fisher-transformed difference test, p<0.001. Comparing low-contrast normal with high-contrast blind trials still favored normal monitoring, 0.45 versus 0.25, p<0.005, despite higher blind-field discrimination performance.

Descriptions of earlier static-stimulus studies distinguish absent visual phenomenology from awareness of stimulus presence. The authors also allow subjective nonvisual experience to accompany successful blind-field judgments.

claims.downstream_use: Y is metacognitive allocation of postdecision wagers: choosing payment contingent on discrimination correctness rather than a coin flip. Its accuracy-coupling demonstrates monitoring beyond merely registering X.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Retain as a bounded single-patient prospect. Human judgment: is the same-day, condition-level visibility-to-wager transfer sufficiently persuasive for an association between visual access and monitoring, despite lesion-dependent processing differences?
claims.remaining_alternative: The intact field could supply more reliable trialwise evidence or different decision cues despite matched average accuracy. Report-conditioned accuracies differed, and lesion, hemisphere, wagering strategy, or nonvisual confidence could affect monitoring. Physical contrast reversal does not match internal evidence or isolate awareness.
claims.supported_claim: In GY, the hemifield with more reported visual awareness supported better accuracy-sensitive postdecision wagering, despite approximately matched overall visual discrimination.
claims.x_and_existence: X is visual information specifying whether the vertical grating occupies the upper or lower quadrant. Above-chance discrimination establishes its availability in both fields, including blind-field trials reported as guesses; this establishes usable content, not unconsciousness by itself.

claims.awareness_evidence: The neural comparison inherits the condition-level awareness evidence and transfer limitations above; it is not a trialwise contrast of equally accurate seen and unseen judgments.
claims.comparison: Normal-versus-blind activation was tested under titrated overall accuracy. The narrower correct-unseen comparison was also attempted, but its estimate and effective comparison coverage are not reported.
claims.contribution_reasoning: These findings constrain neural interpretations based only on superior average discrimination, but BOLD activation is not demonstrated downstream mental use. The attempted correct-unseen analysis remains unresolved rather than supporting a negative finding. Neither widespread activation nor the uncorrected amygdala observation establishes broadcast, flexibility, or emotional processing.

decisive_evidence.observation: Normal-field stimulation produced greater prefrontal/parietal activity, with reported clusters corrected at p<0.05. The blind-greater-than-normal amygdala cluster did not survive correction, p=0.289.

The authors report reduced power and nothing systematic for blind correct-unseen versus normal correct-unseen trials, without contrast estimates. They acknowledge preparatory flexibility, weak-signal amplification, and metacognition as alternative activation interpretations.

claims.downstream_use: No additional behavioral Y is established by the activation contrasts. Up/Down performance measures direct registration; the separately demonstrated downstream function is wagering-based monitoring.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Keep as neural context. Human check: are activation differences being substituted for evidence that awareness changes a tested downstream function?
claims.remaining_alternative: Hemisphere, lesion-related reorganization, weak-input processing, reporting demands, or metacognitive differences could contribute to the activation pattern.
claims.supported_claim: Greater normal-field prefrontal/parietal activity survives approximate first-order performance matching, but does not itself establish another awareness-to-function mapping.
claims.x_and_existence: The same grating-location information is available in both regimes. Neural localization does not establish a separate information-bearing content or mental function.

assessment.paper_reason: The article contains its own interpretable behavioral awareness–use comparison: greater reported visual access accompanies better metacognitive wagering under active, achieved discrimination-performance control. Its value is bounded by separate reporting blocks and single-patient, lesion-dependent processing. Neural findings remain context.
reading_gaps: Original Persaud and Lau (2008) and Schurger et al. (2006, 2008) studies are unavailable; their awareness evidence is known only through this article’s descriptions.
Contrast-specific visibility rates, raw observations, and plotted figure images were not supplied. All supplied article text, table entries, and captions were read.

claims.awareness_evidence: The actual instruction was to discriminate Gabor presence from absence, not report subjective visibility or an experienced conjunction. Calibration used 200 trials and a staircase intended to drive detection to chance. After binding, detection was tested at the binding-task mask strength without feedback; two participants with replicated above-chance performance were excluded. This concerns the item carrying X, so it is a plausible indirect availability check, not a known unrelated-content measure. However, nonsignificance for retained individuals does not establish unawareness, and achieved detection estimates are not reported. Ineffective masking is described as allowing conscious processing, but no corresponding S1 awareness result is supplied. Transfer from the post-task detection test to incidental S1 processing is therefore bounded.
claims.comparison: The within-participant comparison changed mask proximity to S1: ineffective masking inserted 100-ms blank screens around it. Target type and mask strength were shared, and S1–S2 timing was equated. Individual calibration supports mask effectiveness, but it did not match internal signal strength across regimes. The comparison is plausibly visibility-related rather than a verified conscious-versus-unconscious split.
claims.contribution_reasoning: The useful contribution is the joint feature-dependent effect after effectively masked S1, together with an actual masking-by-binding comparison and a broader same-experiment analysis—not simply faster responses after less effective masking. These observations provisionally challenge complete disappearance of joint-feature carryover under effective masking. The stricter analysis is interpretable for its selected participants because its rules and results are reported, but the broader analysis weakens masked-only detection. Nondetection of moderation remains informative only as an uncertain comparison, not evidence of equality. Results 2 is a reanalysis, not an independent replication; the article’s stronger necessity conclusion is not retained.

decisive_evidence.observation: Reported binding costs were 5.8 ms after effectively masked S1, t(27)=1.8, p=.04 one-tailed, and 8.6 ms after ineffectively masked S1. The direct masking-by-orientation-by-location test was F(1,27)=0.25, p>.6.

Including initially excluded poor performers made both regime-specific RT costs nonsignificant, ps>.08. Removing RT cutoffs preserved the overall orientation-by-location interaction, F(1,33)=4.7, p<.05, but neither regime-specific planned comparison was significant. Masking moderation remained undetected, F(1,33)=0.31, p>.55.

Presence/absence detection calibrated masks before binding and evaluated them afterward. Binding used the final calibration strength increased by 10%; two participants passed both above-chance screening stages and were excluded. No retained-group detection estimate or ineffective-S1 awareness test is reported.

Ineffectively masked S1 produced faster but slightly less accurate S2 responses. Accuracy also showed no detected masking modulation of the joint feature interaction in the broader analysis, F(1,33)=0.33, p>.5; this does not establish equivalence.

claims.downstream_use: Participants judged S2 orientation. Dependence of that later response on the joint repetition or alternation of S1 orientation and location indicates use of earlier information, rather than direct registration of S1. Conservatively, Y is joint-feature-dependent carryover into later orientation decisions, consistent with binding, short-term maintenance and retrieval considered together—not separately demonstrated capacities.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Retain as a tentative supplementary prospect. Human vetting should judge whether indirect item-presence evidence and the selected-sample masked effect provide useful constraint despite missing ineffective-S1 awareness verification and weakened regime-specific results. That judgment should not treat nonsignificant moderation as equivalence or require a unique binding mechanism.
claims.remaining_alternative: Residual conscious access and weaker effective-S1 evidence could produce a smaller, noisier carryover effect. Location-dependent orientation priming could also mimic binding. The point estimates remain compatible with scalar attenuation; the null interaction does not defeat that account or establish an independent causal role for awareness.
claims.supported_claim: Joint orientation–location carryover into later judgments was detected after effectively masked S1 in the stricter analysis. Broader analysis preserved joint carryover overall, but not separate detection within either masking regime. Neither analysis detected masking-dependent modulation: a bounded awareness-use prospect, not proof that consciousness is unnecessary or effects are equal.
claims.x_and_existence: X is S1 orientation and spatial-position information, not awareness of an already-composed conjunction. Presented Gabors supplied both features; the joint repetition effect supports usable feature information across the experiment, with weaker regime-specific evidence after effective masking. The awareness check concerns the source item; it does not establish conscious experience of its bound relation.

assessment.paper_reason: The article contains its own relevant experiment and an interpretable, though fragile, joint-feature comparison. Its value survives as tentative comparative evidence after integrating the less selective analysis, without adopting the authors’ necessity or equality claims.
reading_gaps: Only extracted article text and figure captions were supplied; graphical panels and any underlying data were unavailable.

Tables 1–2 duplicate the ineffective-mask label across both blocks. Reported exclusions do not fully reconcile with df-implied analysis sizes. Detection estimates, ineffective-S1 awareness results and uncertainty intervals for the critical difference are unreported.

claims.awareness_evidence: Participants first discriminated the later target orientation, then rated perception of the preceding colored circle 0 (not visible at all) to 3 (clearly visible). Experiments 1/2 had 53%/39% cue-present rating-0 trials; nonzero ratings defined aware trials, and rating-3-only analyses reportedly gave similar Experiment-1 results. Experiment 2 added a separate 100-trial cue-localization block: rating-0 accuracy 25.07% (SE 3.24%), t<1, against 25% chance. This converges with subjective reports but does not prove exhaustive invisibility or first-order matching; replacing target response by cue localization changes attention/task demands. Experiment 3 used a coarser binary cue report; the authors explicitly acknowledge partial-awareness contamination. Its different timing and suppression do not inherit the Experiment-2 validation.
claims.comparison: Experiments 1 and 2: matching-color same-versus-different-location benefit, compared between visibility 0 and visibility 1–3; Experiment 3: same-color benefit compared between saw/did-not-see trials.
claims.contribution_reasoning: Located positive unaware effects plus actual direct nondifference tests offer more than an unaware-only priming result. Physical settings and task demands remain fixed within experiments. The useful constraint is that strong spatial capture can coexist with reported invisibility and did not measurably grow with reported visibility here; uncertain internal evidence and limited null precision bound that claim.

decisive_evidence.observation: Matching-color benefits: aware 50 ms (SE 10.35), unaware 36 ms (SE 10.62); both positive, direct difference F(1,52)=1.76,p>.19.
Benefits 55/40 ms aware/unaware; direct difference F<1. Null-rated cue localization was 25.07% (SE 3.24%).
Same-color benefits 104 ms in both regimes (SE 11/12), both p<.0001; direct difference F<1. Binary visibility may conceal partial awareness.

claims.downstream_use: Spatial attentional capture by a task-relevant cue, operationalized as improved subsequent-target orientation-response time when target and cue share location. This is use of earlier X in selecting a later target, rather than a direct cue report.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Retain as a descriptive preserved-capture prospect. Does the author judge subjective colored-circle visibility sufficiently content aligned for spatial/color-contingent capture, given delayed reporting and the explicit binary-report limitation? Do not treat nonsignificance as equality.
claims.remaining_alternative: Internal cue evidence was not matched, cue reporting followed the target response, report criterion/retention can sort trials, and the binary report has acknowledged sensitivity limits. No equivalence margin or positive null evidence was supplied.
claims.supported_claim: Task-relevant spatial cueing is demonstrable on trials reported as unseen, and these experiments detected no awareness-linked change in its magnitude. This is descriptive preservation within this paradigm, not equivalence.
claims.x_and_existence: X is the pretarget colored-circle cue, including its spatial position and color relevant to the search set. It was physically presented under the same duration/suppression settings in both reported regimes. Color-contingent location effects on a later target establish use beyond cue registration.

claims.awareness_evidence: The same trialwise colored-circle reports described above concern the focal cue. Higher reports reflect conscious cue experience rather than a manipulated signal increment, but endogenous internal strength and report differences remain. Experiment-2 objective validation adds bounded convergence; Experiment-3 binary reports explicitly allow partial awareness.
claims.comparison: Preserve the focal color-relation × cue-location mapping in each physical experiment. Experiments 1/2 compare relevant and irrelevant cue colors; Experiment 3 compares same and different cue-target colors during singleton search, crossed with reported visibility.
claims.contribution_reasoning: The fixed-setting aware/unaware contrasts and their full factorial structure provide a source-grounded association worth vetting despite weak signal control. Experiment 3 supplies a directly motivated contrary net-benefit pattern; it cannot silently confer diagnostic control on Experiments 1/2 or on the standalone cost claim. The article constrains operational spatial selection more securely than object-file updating as a unique mechanism.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Experiments 1 and 2 color × location × awareness results
decisive_evidence.observation: Omnibus interactions F(4,52)=14.99 and F(4,44)=12.30. Irrelevant-color costs were 33 versus 1 ms and 35 versus 2 ms aware/unaware; direct differences p<.04 in each experiment.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Experiment 3 planned control and critical results
decisive_evidence.observation: Same-color benefits 104/104 ms, different-color benefits 8/43 ms aware/unaware. Omnibus F(4,45)=13.74,p<.0001; different-color direct contrast F(1,45)=3.92,p<.055. This trend is not a conventionally significant isolated difference.

Object-updating interpretation relies on earlier continuity findings not supplied here. Note 1 acknowledges the unexpected same/different-color disparity within unseen trials and attributes it to partial awareness.

claims.downstream_use: Color-dependent spatial guidance of subsequent target selection: cue-target position changes the response benefit/cost differently depending on color relation. Capture and same-location costs are components of this common operational mapping; object-file updating is a proposed mechanism, with inhibition/disengagement alternatives.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Retain the whole mapping and qualified component results. Is Experiment 3 sufficient to challenge the independently justified simple same-Y scalar account, given its p<.055 component contrast and acknowledged contamination, or should its E classification remain physical-only? Earlier continuity experiments would be required to make a stronger object-file-specific claim.
claims.remaining_alternative: Experiments 1/2 can reflect stronger amplification of both signed effects. Experiment 3 is consistent with selective strengthening of a mismatch cost superimposed on capture; whether the whole mapping meets the frozen diagnostic scalar-account criterion needs explicit scoped review. Earlier continuity evidence is unavailable for a specific object-file mechanism, and Experiment-3 partial awareness prevents a necessity claim.
claims.supported_claim: Reported awareness is associated with a changed color-dependent spatial-selection profile. The Experiment-3 planned reduction in net benefit for seen different-color cues challenges a simple account predicting uniform strengthening of positive cueing, but its component contrast is imprecise and the underlying mixture of capture and mismatch cost remains unresolved.
claims.x_and_existence: The same pretarget colored circle provides color and position for the subsequent selection mapping. Experiment-3 target color is unpredictable, so different-color cues remain task relevant; they must not be equated with the ignored cues of Experiments 1/2.

assessment.paper_reason: A useful same-cue awareness/use comparison: physically fixed liminal cues were grouped by trialwise subjective visibility while subsequent-target spatial cueing was measured. Relevant-color capture survives reported invisibility with directly tested descriptive nondifferences; irrelevant/different-color cueing changes across visibility. This supports a bounded functional profile, without establishing equality, awareness causation or necessity of consciousness for object-file formation.
reading_gaps: All supplied extracted text units page:1–page:12 were read. Graphical source pixels were not provided; axes, captions and text were read, but Figure-4 higher-rating accuracy values cannot be recovered precisely from text.
Supplement inventory has not been independently verified; no additional supplement text was supplied.

Carmel & Lamy (2014) continuity controls and the brief-exposure pilot were described but originals/data were not supplied. The conservative spatial-selection claim does not require their object-file mechanism to be established.

Experiment-2 accuracy prose is internally inconsistent: p.6 states more errors for aware trials, followed by a sentence saying fewer errors when consciously perceived; Table 1 and the first statement support more errors overall. RT claims are separated from that inconsistency.

claims.awareness_evidence: Participants were trained to signal recognition of a commission error with a right-button response on the immediately following Go trial instead of the usual left response. This directly concerns the prior action's erroneous status, not merely stimulus visibility. However, operational classification counted any deviation from the usual response as awareness; an ordinary left response counted as unawareness. Thus, reported errors plausibly indicate conscious access, whereas unreported errors could include missed reports or attentional lapses. Awareness of the erroneous letter's identity was not separately measured. The article's description of reduced awareness in Hester et al. is secondary evidence from an unavailable original, not validation of these classifications.
claims.comparison: Within participants, later inhibition was compared following reported versus unreported errors, separately for same-letter and different-letter No-Go opportunities. Stimuli lasted 700 ms with a 600-ms interval throughout; successive No-Go events were separated by four to twelve Go trials. Presentation settings were fixed, but internal attention, encoding strength and error evidence were not matched or titrated.
claims.contribution_reasoning: This is a useful bounded prospect because an immediate, content-aligned error report predicts later performance selectively when the previously failed situation recurs. The task's instructed error-dependent contingency supplies a concrete route by which knowledge of having erred can guide later inhibition. The result goes beyond comparing stronger and weaker physical presentations. Nevertheless, the awareness-by-context interaction does not eliminate stronger internal registration or attention as a common cause. The fully reported group interaction supplies an informative nondetection, not equivalence: awareness-related correction was not demonstrably different between users and controls. Cannabis-use moderation adds heterogeneity without establishing cannabis causation.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Methods 2.3 and 2.4.1: reporting instruction, contingency and outcome model
decisive_evidence.observation: Errors were signalled on the next Go trial. After 75% of first-presentation errors, the next No-Go repeated the failed letter; after correct inhibition, it always differed. Participants knew this contingency. Models predicted inhibition on that later No-Go.

decisive_evidence.observation: For N=70, awareness-by-trial-type OR was 1.76, 95% CI [1.07, 2.89]; the narrative identifies better same-stimulus inhibition after aware errors. Awareness-by-group OR was 0.96 [0.57, 1.62]. In the 36 users, same-stimulus correction showed awareness-by-CUI β=-0.67 [-1.21, -0.14] and awareness-by-onset β=-0.62 [-1.22, -0.02]. The article describes earlier missed-target priming and contrary behavioral nulls, but those unavailable originals cannot validate awareness here. Thus the contribution is more than significant versus nonsignificant labels: related-context assistance covaries with same-item T2 reportability under fixed presentation settings. Replication across display durations and response formats adds bounded robustness. The incorrect-report findings constrain observed facilitation in those settings, but low T3 accuracy limits sensitivity; they establish neither equivalence nor consciousness as necessary.

decisive_evidence.observation: On T1-correct trials, related/unrelated T3 accuracy was 67.50%/58.84% with T2 correct and 6.94%/8.12% with T2 incorrect. The T2-performance × context interaction was F(1,24)=25.22, p<.001. The incorrect-T2 relatedness test was nonsignificant, p=.120.

Related/unrelated T3 accuracy was 44.04%/35.37% with T2 correct and 11.19%/11.20% with T2 incorrect. The interaction was F(1,24)=7.89, p=.010; the incorrect-T2 relatedness test had p=.99. Words appeared for 15 ms, versus 70 ms in Experiment 1, with the same 90-ms item cycle.

claims.awareness_evidence: Immediately after cueing, participants localized the annulus left/right, instructed to “attend to the circle, not the dot” and respond accurately. The masked instruction described one circle appearing earlier. This addresses X but measures registration, not subjective experience. Visible accuracy was 97.8%; selected masked accuracy was 49.30%, p=.46. Chance-based selection and nonsignificance do not prove unawareness. Experiment 2 improves transfer through matched trial sequences and visible practice previews, but remains a separate posttask sample. Sixteen excluded masked observers averaged 72.28% accuracy while generally reporting inability to see the cue; these informal reports concern a different subgroup and challenge accuracy-as-awareness classification. Jointly, the access contrast is plausible, not a validated phenomenal separation.
claims.comparison: Experiment 1 compared 20 red, unmasked-cue observers with 24 of 40 black, masked-cue observers meeting the authors’ chance criterion. Cue locations were fixed or randomized; presentation strength and participants were not matched across visibility regimes.
claims.contribution_reasoning: The same visible cues facilitated targets when their locations varied, so their fixed-location failure was not general cue impotence. The schedule-specific pattern adds information beyond stronger input simply producing greater facilitation. Replication and the longer-SOA control constrain sensitivity and timing explanations, without matching internal evidence or identifying an awareness-specific mechanism.

decisive_evidence.observation: Fixed-cue facilitation was 15.7 ms for selected masked observers, p<.001, versus 2.1 ms for visible observers, p=.407; validity×visibility F(1,42)=14.00, p=.001. Random-cue facilitation was 14.9 and 14.2 ms respectively, both p<.001; these estimates do not establish equivalence.
The 16 above-chance masked observers generally reported not seeing the cue and showed 8.5-ms fixed-cue facilitation. Their intermediate result is not an established graded-awareness comparison.

Experiment 2 matched 420-trial sequences across cueing and localization: 13 chance-selected observers averaged 49.39% localization and showed 15.6-ms fixed-cue facilitation, p=.001. Experiment 3’s 20 retained visible observers showed −2.9-ms facilitation at 100-ms SOA, p=.317.

Misses were below 1%; reported correlations did not detect associations between false alarms and spatial RT differences. This weakens a simple response-propensity explanation but does not eliminate decision dynamics.

Independent awareness causality would require additional experimental control.
claims.remaining_alternative: Effective cue strength could amplify competing inhibition or adaptation and thereby reduce net facilitation. Color, masking effectiveness, duration and participants differ; residual awareness and task transfer remain uncertain. Neither the inversion nor interaction eliminates this awareness-independent signal account.
claims.supported_claim: Repeated masked spatial cues produced greater facilitation of later dot detection than salient unmasked cues: a useful provisional awareness–use comparison concerning net spatial prioritization.
claims.x_and_existence: X is the earlier annulus’s left/right location. It was physically instantiated in both regimes; spatially specific target facilitation supports usable location information under masking, without establishing its conscious availability or neural format.

claims.awareness_evidence: The same content-aligned posttask localization evidence and limitations apply. The comparison concerns access to cue location during exposure, inferred retrospectively—not conscious knowledge of repetition or awareness of a remembered regularity.

claims.downstream_use: Y is persistent location-dependent prioritization when the cue is no longer present.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Use as context, not a separate prospect. Human judgment: can it help explain the immediate dissociation without borrowing that mapping’s inverted pattern to promote this stronger-induction/larger-aftereffect comparison?

claims.x_and_existence: X remains earlier cue location. Old/new RT differences establish retained influence after visible exposure; masked nondetection does not establish that retained location information was absent.

At unchanged 33 ms in E6, 67% of participants reporting seeing cues after being informed reached the 80% success criterion.

Experiment 3 used one nominal cue luminance within 40-trial blocks, but adjusted monitor brightness between blocks to maintain mixed seeing. Neither design matched internal cue evidence across report groups.

Experiment 2's report-conditioned reversal survives important task, target-visibility and eye-movement controls. Experiment 3 contributes positive longer-delay comparisons using a single nominal cue luminance, while its short-delay result establishes cue-side use without reported seeing. Its longer-delay nonreplication bounds the persistence of that facilitation. decisive_evidence.observation: Among 14 retained observers, expected meant opposite the cue and unexpected meant the cue side. Seen-trial RTs were 459 versus 489 ms; unseen-trial RTs were 566 versus 550 ms. The awareness-by-location interaction was F(1,13)=23.22, p<.001; both simple cueing effects were significant. Error results showed no apparent speed–accuracy trade-off.

Awareness-by-location interactions were significant at both delays (p<.01); unseen location contrasts were nonsignificant (Fs<1). Thus persistent unseen cue-side facilitation did not replicate.

At 80 ms, unseen expected/unexpected RTs were 602/572 ms, with a significant cue-side benefit, F(1,7)=16.37, p<.01. Seen means were 576/561 ms; the awareness-by-location interaction was F<1, not evidence of equality. The cue lasted 15 ms, followed by the target after the stated 500-ms delay; observers then reported seeing/not seeing. Experiment 1 showed a cueing reversal (interaction p<.01), but illumination, target visibility, block order and report-task requirements differed between regimes, making this weaker corroboration.

claims.downstream_use: Y is spatial prioritization supporting later X/O identification. Location-dependent target RTs demonstrate use of earlier cue information, rather than direct cue detection. The instructed opposite-side rule was shared task knowledge, not the focal awareness comparison.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Retain as a bounded supporting prospect. Human judgment: is the report-conditioned spatial pattern useful for the intended synthesis despite unmatched internal evidence and delayed, target-sensitive reports, without interpreting awareness as independently causal?
claims.remaining_alternative: Weaker or slower cue evidence could still facilitate the cue side while failing to support instructed opposite-side allocation, producing the crossover without a causal role for awareness. Report criterion, retention and target-induced masking also remain alternatives. Experiment 2 excluded one observer with excessive unseen-trial errors, restricting inference to the retained population. The longer-delay nulls do not establish equivalence, zero capacity or necessity. Distinguishing awareness from these alternatives would require additional controlled evidence.
claims.supported_claim: Reported seeing of a lateralized cue accompanies instructed opposite-side benefits in later target identification; cue-side facilitation can occur without reported seeing. The relation depends on delay and experimental setting, rather than showing that awareness is necessary for spatial orienting.
claims.x_and_existence: X is the occurrence and side of the peripheral bar. It was physically presented in both report regimes. Cue-location-dependent target performance establishes usable spatial information on unseen Experiment 2 trials and unseen short-delay Experiment 3 trials. Longer-delay unseen nulls do not independently establish that the information remained available. No particular neural representation is required.

assessment.paper_reason: The article contains its own interpretable, content-linked subjective-awareness comparisons of downstream spatial use. Their bounded value survives the contrary longer-delay findings, but does not establish independent causation by awareness.
reading_gaps: No separate supplement or cited original experiments were supplied; their descriptions remain secondary context.

The extraction contains inconsistent Experiment 3 omnibus significance signs, degrees of freedom and aggregate seeing percentages. No page images or trial-level data were supplied to resolve these; the assessment relies on tables and explicit SOA-specific contrasts.

claims.awareness_evidence: After each response window, participants reported whether they had initially looked in the correct direction. Recorded errors reported as incorrect were classified as aware; those reported as correct were classified as unaware. This directly addresses initial-response error content. Reports followed a 1000-ms response window, during a 2000-ms rating period; retention, correction and reporting biases remain possible. The 3% false-alarm rate supports report specificity, not perfect sensitivity.
claims.comparison: The comparison uses naturally occurring errors within the same task and participants, not manipulated awareness. Acquisition of error evidence was not matched: aware errors had larger initial saccades than unaware errors, 7.5° versus 6.0°. Nonsignificant latency and RCZ differences do not establish matched internal signals.
claims.contribution_reasoning: Trial-specific, content-aligned reports and an actual between-category accuracy contrast provide a bounded association beyond an externally stronger-input/larger-effect comparison. However, the result supports next-trial accuracy, not the authors’ broader claim that awareness enables the entire speed–accuracy adjustment function. Whole-sample slowing was not detected, and the nine participants selected for showing slowing cannot independently establish an awareness-specific effect.

decisive_evidence.observation: In 13 participants, next-trial error rates were 12.49% ± 2.8 after aware errors and 18.79% ± 3.9 after unaware errors, T = −2.07, p = 0.03. Group post-error slowing was nonsignificant overall and for both error categories, ps > 0.344.
Initial wrong-direction saccades counted as errors even when immediately corrected; awareness reports explicitly concerned the initial direction.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Introduction; Error awareness and post-error adjustments
decisive_evidence.observation: The article describes contrary earlier slowing findings from Endrass et al., while its Discussion claims adjustments occurred only after aware errors. Those descriptions do not override the focal whole-sample slowing results.

claims.downstream_use: Accuracy on trial N+1 is subsequent action performance, distinct from detecting or reporting the error on trial N.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Retain as an associational prospect: is this within-task accuracy difference useful despite uncontrolled error-signal strength and serial attentional state?
claims.remaining_alternative: Stronger error evidence, better ongoing attention, or effects of the different report responses could produce both acknowledged errors and better subsequent performance without awareness independently enabling adjustment.
claims.supported_claim: Explicitly acknowledged antisaccade errors were followed by fewer errors on the next trial than unacknowledged errors.
claims.x_and_existence: X is the initial gaze–goal mismatch: looking toward the peripheral stimulus despite the instruction to look away. Eye tracking establishes erroneous actions in both report regimes.

claims.awareness_evidence: The same initial-direction instruction tracks this X, including corrected errors. Nevertheless, reporting occurs after correction, so nonacknowledgment does not establish absence of transient awareness during the corrective movement.
claims.comparison: Both categories contain recorded initial errors. Their correction probabilities are directly compared, but saccade amplitude and endogenous evidence differ; no achieved signal matching was demonstrated.
claims.contribution_reasoning: This supplies a distinct, plausible online motor-use comparison across retrospective access to the same error content. It shows that report-defined unawareness accompanies substantial corrective performance. Its reverse association is informative for correction itself, not a signal-control argument for next-trial accuracy.

decisive_evidence.observation: Unaware errors were corrected more frequently than aware errors: 76.0% ± 5.6 versus 59.3% ± 7.9, T = −2.54, p = 0.03. Corrected initial errors remained classified as errors.

claims.downstream_use: Immediate corrective gaze movement is a plausible motor adjustment resolving the initial gaze–goal discrepancy.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Retain provisionally: is corrective reorientation sufficiently diagnostic of using the initial mismatch to merit supplementary awareness–use value?
claims.remaining_alternative: Correction could reflect completion of an already prepared antisaccade rather than feedback from the initial error; correction could also obscure later recollection of that error.
claims.supported_claim: Recorded errors later denied in the awareness report were often corrected, and more frequently than acknowledged errors.
claims.x_and_existence: X remains the initial erroneous gaze relative to the instructed goal—not peripheral-stimulus information or a broadened response program. Recorded errors and subsequent corrections establish a behaviorally resolvable mismatch.

claims.awareness_evidence: Reports measured awareness of the initial action error, not awareness of bodily changes.
claims.comparison: Aware and unaware errors differed in insular activity; RCZ activity did not significantly differ. Neither finding establishes matched error information or a downstream autonomic function.
claims.contribution_reasoning: These are useful neural-registration and awareness-correlate observations, but the proposed autonomic/interoceptive explanation lacks measured bodily responses and bodily-awareness reports. It therefore does not supply another empirical awareness–use mapping.

decisive_evidence.observation: Left insular activity was greater for aware errors, T = 4.34, p < 0.0001; the RCZ contrast was nonsignificant, T = 1.32, p = 0.211. Pupillary recording was technically unavailable, and autonomic explanations were explicitly speculative.

claims.downstream_use: No autonomic outcome was measured; regional BOLD differences alone do not demonstrate downstream use.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Keep as mechanistic context, not a functional prospect.
claims.remaining_alternative: Insular activity could reflect stronger error evidence, autonomic implementation, or awareness rather than a demonstrated causal pathway.
claims.supported_claim: Error acknowledgment covaried with insular activity, but autonomic use was not established.
claims.x_and_existence: Initial-error content is established; the hypothesized visceral content was not measured.

REF_G17.title: Adaptation following errors: Error awareness predicts future performance

claims.awareness_evidence: Participants were trained to signal recognition of a commission error with a right-button response on the immediately following Go trial, before the later inhibition outcome. This instruction addresses conscious recognition that their own action was erroneous, not merely visibility of the letter. However, the analysis classified any departure from the left-on-error/left-on-following-Go pattern as aware. Signalling failures, delayed recognition and unrelated deviations could therefore contaminate both categories. The defensible comparison is between errors classified as reported/aware and unreported/unaware, not independently verified conscious and wholly unconscious error representations.
claims.comparison: The groups shared stimulus durations, task instructions and error-recurrence rules; awareness was observed rather than manipulated. This provides a bounded comparison without deliberately increasing stimulus strength, but neither exact item matching nor matched internal evidence was demonstrated. Subject/block random effects address clustering, not momentary attention or error-signal strength. Nonsignificant response-speed and interval differences do not establish matching. The different-letter estimate is interpretable contrary evidence against an unrestricted benefit, but its confidence interval includes substantial benefits, including the same-letter estimate. Separate significant and nonsignificant models do not establish an awareness-by-recurrence interaction.
claims.contribution_reasoning: The trained, temporally prior error report and subsequent inhibitory outcome form a plausible content-aligned awareness–use comparison. The task supplies a concrete opportunity for error information to guide later action, and recurrence improves stopping overall. Thus, the result contributes an interpretable association between reported error recognition and delayed corrective control, rather than merely documenting stronger physical input producing a larger effect. The different-letter estimate and response-speed controls bound general-caution interpretations. They do not establish that awareness uniquely causes adaptation, that its benefit is exclusively stimulus-specific, or that error information was used without awareness.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Participants; Results and Table 2, same-stimulus model
decisive_evidence.observation: In the 51-participant study, awareness classification predicted successful inhibition on the next same-letter No-Go: β = 0.50, 95% CI [0.13, 0.83], OR = 1.64 [1.14, 2.30]. Reported correction rates were 78% after aware versus 65% after unaware errors.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Behavioural task and No-Go event classification
decisive_evidence.observation: Error recognition was signalled on the following Go trial. After 75% of first-presentation errors, the next No-Go repeated the failed letter, which could not appear on intervening Go trials. No-Go trials were separated by 4–12 Go trials; stimuli lasted 700 ms with a 600-ms interval.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Results, different-stimulus model; final Discussion limitation
decisive_evidence.observation: Overall post-error stopping was higher for same-letter than different-letter trials, 75.26% versus 48.92%. For different-letter trials, the awareness estimate was β = 0.06 [-0.46, 0.60], OR = 1.06 [0.63, 1.90]. The authors note substantially fewer such trials and uncertainty introduced by the dominant recurrence contingency.

decisive_evidence.location_detail: Pre-No-Go reaction-time results; Discussion of signalling interference
decisive_evidence.observation: Awareness did not detectably predict reaction time immediately before the subsequent No-Go, β = -4.11, 95% CI [-23.78, 15.56]. Some early post-error comparisons showed speeding rather than slowing, but the authors acknowledge that the awareness response interferes with response-speed measurement.

claims.downstream_use: Y is successful withholding on a later No-Go under an error-dependent recurrence contingency, not the response used to register or report the original error. Participants knew an error usually predicted recurrence of its letter. The recurrence advantage and awareness-conditioned stopping association support delayed corrective control, although they do not uniquely identify learning, explicit prediction or the representation used.
claims.reason_and_vetting_question: Retain as a bounded observational prospect. Human vetting should judge whether the trained report instruction and prospective timing support a sufficiently credible awareness comparison despite broad classification and the signalling action itself.
claims.remaining_alternative: Stronger endogenous error evidence or better attention could jointly increase report likelihood, retention of the failed letter and later inhibition. Signalling could also rehearse or mark the error. These explanations survive the speed controls; separating them from an independent awareness contribution requires additional experimental control, not simply rereading.
claims.supported_claim: Commission errors classified as aware were more often followed by successful inhibition when the failed letter recurred. This supports awareness-associated delayed corrective performance, not proof that consciousness causes learning or is necessary for correction.
claims.x_and_existence: X is the occurrence of one's own commission error: responding to a repeated letter when withholding was required. Objective commission errors occurred in both report categories. Their occurrence establishes an information-bearing event, but does not independently establish internal registration of error content on unreported trials. X is not reformulated as conscious knowledge of letter identity or the predictive contingency, neither of which was separately measured.

assessment.paper_reason: The article contains its own interpretable, content-aligned prospective comparison. Its contribution is awareness-associated delayed inhibitory adaptation. The different-letter nondetection limits, but does not prove, task specificity; response-speed observations serve as controls rather than a separate adaptation claim.
reading_gaps: The described OSF data and code were not supplied; report-compliance details cannot be independently checked.
Cited original motor and anti-saccade studies were unavailable. Their mixed findings remain secondary descriptions, not independent validation of this awareness measure.
Only extracted text and figure captions were supplied; figure artwork was not inspected.
